Comma use is very much a style thing, there are few hard and fast rules in English and organizations like universities and news papers will have published style guides so that editors and writers can apply commas the way the chief editors want them applied. Commas communicate a pause or break in the sentence or help to join 2 inter-related ideas, or communicate or clarify something about an idea which is sort of an aside to the main idea.

Just from looking at your examples above, a comma is not necessary to use any time AND or BUT or IF or WHICH or AND. I've worked in marketing and advertising for years and the general rule of thumb here is to never use a comma unless you absolutely need to as commas are speed bumps in communicating an idea, use them and all other punctuation as little as possible.

But, tldr is more often than not comma use is based on preferred writing style. If I were to re-write your super sentence:

Contrary to popular belief the monetary reform is an important but by no means necessary topic which we will discuss and the secretary of state will not stop us.

The same idea is communicated with all the commas removed.

Contrary to popular belief the monetary reform is an important but by no means necessary topic which we will discuss, and the secretary of stat will not stop us.
